name: Run storm and major event response
summary: When a storm, a lightning burst or the loss of a transmission supply knocks out power to many customers at once, the utility shifts from routine outage handling to a major event response. In most events the control room calls out the on-call roster and restores 90% of customers within hours; in a few it activates incident command, sends out damage assessors, brings in contractors and other utilities' crews and runs restoration in 12- to 16-hour periods for days. Afterwards the event is confirmed as a Major Event Day and reported to the OEB. It is hard because warnings are unreliable, damage is unknown for hours, and crews, material and public communications all have to scale at once.

baseline.org_archetype: A city-owned Ontario electricity distributor with about 350,000 customers, a 24-hour system control centre, overhead and underground line crews and single-person trouble trucks, using SCADA, an outage management system, smart meters and mobile workforce tablets.
baseline.notes: Modelled on Hydro Ottawa Limited's published major event reports, scorecard and news releases for 2019-2022; the organisation chart, headcounts and wages come from the organisation file.

trigger: A forecast severe storm, a sudden flood of SCADA alarms and outage calls, or a transmission supply loss that takes out many customers at once.
end_state: Customers are restored and the system is back to normal, outside crews are released, and the major event report is filed with the OEB and published.

volume.seasonality: Six of the nine 2019-2022 events fell between April and July (thunderstorms, flooding, wind); others in March, October, November and December.

evidence.note: Nine major events in 48 months (three in 2019, two in 2020, one in 2021, three in 2022) = 0.19 a month; low and high reflect one and four events a year.

steps.name: Watch forecasts and supply alerts
steps.description: The system operator watches Environment Canada watches and warnings, the weather service feed and Hydro One notices of planned or forced supply outages, and tells the shift supervisor when severe wind, ice, lightning or a supply problem is expected.

next.condition: severe weather or a planned supply outage expected
no useful warning or warning not acted on

evidence.note: Of nine 2019-2022 major events, three had pre-event action (staff held over in July 2019, planned supply outage notified in October 2020, staff called in ahead of the December 2022 storm); March 2020 and June 2022 had no warning and the May 2022 derecho's severity was not forecast.

steps.name: Decide on pre-event standby
steps.description: The control room shift supervisor, with the on-call manager, decides how many line, cable and control staff to hold past the end of the day or bring in early, and whether contractors should be warned.

evidence.note: Staff placed on standby when severe weather is forecast; four extra PLTs held in July 2019; on-call staff in at 18:00 and all line and underground staff at 06:00 in December 2022.

steps.name: Arrange standby crews
steps.description: The lines supervisor phones crews to stay past shift or report early, moves trucks and material to the service centres closest to the expected damage and confirms the numbers to the control room.

evidence.note: Additional staff on standby and resources relocated ahead of forecast weather (source); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Outages flood the control room
steps.description: SCADA breaker lockouts and station alarms arrive together while the outage management system groups thousands of calls and smart meter last-gasp messages into predicted outages on the control room screens.

evidence.note: Outages began 9 to 24 minutes after the May 2022 watch; in April 2019 84.2% of callers used the IVR. Wait from warning to impact is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Triage alarms and outages
steps.description: Operators on every console sort SCADA lockouts, station and supply alarms and predicted outages, restore what remote switching can, flag wires down for the trouble trucks and estimate how many customers are out and where.

control.basis: Utility Work Protection Code and Electrical Utility Safety Rules (IHSA), required for work on or near distribution lines under the Occupational Health and Safety Act

next.condition: damage on the distribution system only

evidence.note: Five of nine 2019-2022 major events involved loss of supply from Hydro One; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Coordinate supply restoration with Hydro One
steps.description: An operator works with the transmitter's grid control centre on the tripped supply circuit or station, agrees the order of restoring feeders, and transfers load to other stations where capacity allows.

evidence.note: Liaison with Hydro One and the IESO on restoration (posting); supply outages restored in 2 h 40 min (June 2022) and 2 h 41 min (April 2019).

steps.name: Call out the on-call roster
steps.description: The shift supervisor calls out the full on-call roster of line, cable and station trades, trouble responders, supervisors and the on-call manager, and logs who is coming and when.

evidence.note: Event reports state a full on-shift complement and full on-call roster, with 100% of on-call staff used in 2019 events.

steps.name: Decide whether to activate incident command
steps.description: The on-call control manager reviews customers out, the number of outages and the damage reports, and decides whether the control room can run the restoration with on-call crews or the Electrical Emergency Response Plan and an incident command centre must be activated.

next.condition: widespread damage or a long supply outage: activate incident command
control room and on-call crews can manage

evidence.note: Incident command was activated in three of nine 2019-2022 events (July 2019, May 2022, December 2022); April 2019 explicitly did not need the Emergency Response Organization.

steps.name: Open the incident command centre
steps.description: Operations directors and managers take incident command roles (commander, operations, planning, logistics, communications liaison), set up the command room with OMS screens and phone bridges, and set the first operational period and briefing times.

evidence.note: Incident Command Centre staffed 7:30 pm to 2:00 am in July 2019; an Emergency Response Plan with year-round simulations (sources). Roles follow common incident command practice (author's estimate).

steps.name: Organise damage assessment
steps.description: The field services supervisor splits the territory into patrol zones from the OMS and GIS, pairs field service representatives and locators into assessment teams, and issues them maps and a damage recording template on their tablets.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; Hydro Ottawa's After the Storm report lists damage assessment as a strategic priority (from the release; the report itself could not be opened).

steps.name: Patrol and record the damage
steps.description: Assessment teams drive their zones, record broken poles, downed conductors, failed transformers and trees on lines with photos and pole numbers, stand by dangerous wires until a trouble truck arrives, and send results to planning.

evidence.note: More than 1,500 tree contacts and 1,000 outages had to be found in the derecho (source); patrols wait for winds and darkness to pass. Team size and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Set restoration priorities
steps.description: The control manager ranks the work: public safety hazards first, then hospitals, water and other critical services, then feeders and taps with the most customers, and finally single services, and turns the damage list into crew work packages.

evidence.note: Priorities by health and safety risk, essential services such as hospitals and schools, then densely populated areas (source).

steps.name: Decide on outside help
steps.description: The incident commander compares the work packages with the crews available and decides whether to bring in standing-agreement line, forestry and civil contractors and to request mutual assistance crews from other utilities.

next.condition: internal crews and on-call roster are enough

evidence.note: Mutual aid was used only in May 2022 (four utilities plus 11 contractors); one contractor was used in November 2019; contractors with standing agreements were not needed in July 2019.

steps.name: Request contractors and mutual aid
steps.description: The incident commander calls standing-agreement contractors and sends mutual assistance requests through the Electricity Canada and provincial distributors' association channels, stating crew types, equipment, lodging and the expected duration.

evidence.note: Assistance from four neighbouring utilities through Electricity Canada and EDA channels; membership of the Hydro One Mutual Assistance Agreement and the North Atlantic Mutual Aid Group.

steps.name: Outside crews travel in
steps.description: Mutual aid and contractor crews mobilise their trucks and travel to the utility's service centres, which can take most of a day for crews from other cities.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of mobilisation and travel time for crews from neighbouring utilities.

steps.name: Orient outside crews on safety rules
steps.description: Safety advisors brief arriving crews on the host utility's work protection procedures, the control room as controlling authority, radio protocols, local hazards and reporting, and pair each crew with a local guide.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act host-employer duties and the Utility Work Protection Code: outside crews work under the host utility's controlling authority

evidence.note: Outside crews must work under the host's Utility Work Protection Code permits and tags; content and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Stage material and supplies
steps.description: Stores attendants open the warehouse and pole yard around the clock, stage poles, transformers, cross-arms and conductor by service centre, issue material to crews against the event work order and track stock for reorders.

evidence.note: No material shortages in May 2022; a CO2 extinguisher shortage was covered from another station in March 2020. Staffing and hours are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Publish restoration updates
steps.description: Communications advisors post outage counts, restoration progress and safety messages on social media, the website and to media and councillors, and decide whether restoration estimates can be shown as times or must be given in days.

evidence.note: First tweet 26 minutes after the June 2022 start; ETRs to media, shareholders and social media in December 2022; outage map withdrawn and ETRs given in days in May 2022. In events run from the control room, ETRs go out automatically through the OMS and are covered by the control-room restoration step.

steps.name: Run restoration from the control room
steps.description: Without incident command, the shift supervisor and operators dispatch on-call crews and trouble trucks to the predicted outages in priority order, switch customers back as repairs finish, and update estimates until 90% of customers are back.

evidence.note: 90% of customers restored in 6 hours (November 2019), about 8.5 hours (June 2021), 2 h 40 min (June 2022) and 6.8 hours (October 2020) without incident command.

steps.name: Direct one operational period
steps.description: Supervisors brief crews at the start of a 12- to 16-hour operational period, hand out work packages, track completions on the OMS and call in reassignments as damage turns out larger or smaller than assessed.

evidence.note: Restoration ran around the clock with about 450-600 workers in May 2022; 90% restored after about seven days. Period length is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review progress and plan the next period
steps.description: At the end of each period the incident command team reviews customers still out, crew hours and rest needs, material and safety incidents, resets priorities and estimates, and decides whether another period is needed.

next.condition: many customers still out: run another period

evidence.note: Loop share is the author's estimate: one or two periods for the July 2019 and December 2022 events, about 14 for the May 2022 derecho.

steps.name: Return the system to normal
steps.description: Operators work through the temporary switching left by the event, close open points, return feeders to normal configuration, clear tags and make sure temporary repairs are logged for permanent work.

control.basis: Utility Work Protection Code and Electrical Utility Safety Rules (IHSA), required for work on or near distribution lines under the Occupational Health and Safety Act

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice after large events.

steps.name: Stand down and release crews
steps.description: The incident commander or on-call manager releases outside crews, sends staff home under rest rules, closes the command centre and asks each group for its notes, hours and costs.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Hold the lessons-learned debrief
steps.description: Operations, control, safety, stores and communications leads review what worked and what failed, from assessment speed to outage map accuracy, and assign improvement actions.

evidence.note: A company-wide debrief followed the derecho and an After the Storm report was published in November 2022; March 2020 noted continued focus on on-call preparation.

steps.name: Confirm the Major Event Day
steps.description: Once outage records are closed, the regulatory analyst computes the day's system average interruption duration and compares it with the IEEE 1366 threshold built from five years of daily values, and separates loss-of-supply interruptions.

error.defect_description: Customer counts or hours inconsistent between sections of the report (as seen in published reports).

control.basis: OEB reliability reporting using IEEE Standard 1366 major event days

evidence.note: Daily SAIDI 5.97 against threshold 5.3 (November 2019), 12.11 against 5.3 (July 2019), 12.1 against 5.14 (October 2020), 2,308.27 against 5.05 (May 2022), based on IEEE Standard 1366.

steps.name: Draft the major event report
steps.description: The analyst gathers cause, timeline, customers and hours interrupted, staff and contractors used, mutual aid, communications and lessons from operations and communications, and fills in the OEB major event report template.

evidence.note: Reports follow a fixed question set (cause, warning, staffing, mutual aid, communications, IEEE 1366); queue time is the author's estimate within the 60-day filing window.

steps.name: Review the report
steps.description: The control centre manager checks the timeline, restoration times and staffing statements against the OMS and the control log and returns corrections.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve the filing
steps.description: The vice-president of operations reads the reviewed report, checks the statements on preparedness and communications and approves it for filing.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of sign-off for a regulatory filing.

steps.name: File with the OEB and publish
steps.description: The analyst files the major event report with the OEB through its reporting portal and posts the same report on the utility's major events web page.

control.basis: OEB Reporting and Record-keeping Requirements: major event report, normally within 60 days

evidence.note: Reports are filed with the OEB normally within 60 days and published on the major events page.

exceptions.name: Derecho-scale event with mutual aid
exceptions.description: Damage across the whole territory (May 2022: 1,000 outages, 180,946 customers, about 450 workers, four utilities) needs mutual aid, outside-crew orientation and many operational periods; the outage map was withdrawn and estimates given in days.

exceptions.name: Transmission supply loss
exceptions.description: A Hydro One circuit or station trip takes out whole stations; restoration depends on the transmitter and load transfers rather than crews.

exceptions.name: Report sent back for corrections
exceptions.description: The manager finds inconsistent customer counts or times and the analyst redrafts.

benchmarks.unit: hours from event start to 90% of interrupted customers restored
benchmarks.population: Hydro Ottawa major events 2019-2022 where stated

evidence.note: From each event report; November 2019 measured from the main wind damage at 9 am; May 2022 from 3:36 pm May 21 to 6:00 pm May 28.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from event start to the OEB major event report being filed
benchmarks.population: Major events at an Ontario distributor

evidence.note: Reports are filed normally within 60 days of the event (source); the median is the author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Forecasts understate severity, so standby decisions are often too small or too late.

evidence.note: Event reports for May 2022, November 2019 and June 2021 say the weather was more severe than forecast.

pain_points.description: Damage is unknown for hours, so restoration estimates cannot be given and the outage map stops being useful.

evidence.note: Outage map withdrawn during the derecho; damage assessment named a priority after the event.

pain_points.description: Outside crews arrive a day later and need safety orientation and local guides before they are productive.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice.

pain_points.description: Writing the regulatory report weeks later relies on reconstructing times and counts from logs, and published reports contain inconsistent figures.

evidence.note: The December 2022 report gives 67,710 customers interrupted in one place and 31,897 in another.

sources.title: Major events (list of Hydro Ottawa major event reports)
sources.supports: Major events listed by date: three in 2019 (April 15, July 5, November 1), two in 2020 (March 7, October 18), one in 2021 (June 14), three in 2022 (May 21, June 18, December 23); after a major event the utility files a report with the OEB normally within 60 days of occurrence.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Limited Major Event: April 15, 2019
sources.supports: Lightning, flooding and a transformer-station loss of supply; 44,511 customers (13%); station outage restored in 2 h 41 min; no Emergency Response Organization activation; 84.2% of callers used the IVR and 15.8% reached an agent; daily SAIDI 6.14 against 5.3.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Limited Major Event: July 5, 2019
sources.supports: Lightning and loss of supply at four stations; 70,069 customers (21%); longest outage 6 h 35 min; on-call staff, four extra PLTs and control room staff held past end of day; standing service agreements with forestry, civil and lines contractors (not used); Electrical Emergency Response Plan activated with an Incident Command Centre staffed 7:30 pm to 2:00 am; daily SAIDI 12.11 against 5.3.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Limited Major Event: November 1, 2019
sources.supports: Wind storm tree contacts; 14,228 customers (4%); wind damage from 9 am with 90% restored by 3 pm; 100% of on-call staff used and one outside contractor; member of the Hydro One Mutual Assistance Agreement and the North Atlantic Mutual Aid Group; daily SAIDI 5.97 against a threshold of 5.3 based on five years of daily SAIDI.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Limited Major Event: March 7, 2020
sources.supports: Pothead failure and station fire at a municipal station; 11,686 customers (3%); 26 hours to restore all customers of the station; no warning; full on-shift and on-call roster; shortage of CO2 extinguishers covered from another station.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Limited Major Event: October 18, 2020
sources.supports: Planned Hydro One loss of supply to three stations plus a defective-equipment outage; 9,186 customers; 90% restored in 6.8 h; customers notified four days before; dedicated switching crew; weekly preparation meeting for on-call managers; daily SAIDI 12.1 against a threshold of 5.14.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Limited Major Event: June 14, 2021
sources.supports: Lightning; 17,441 customers (5%); 90% restored by 1:04 am the next day (about 8.5 h); storms forecast; full on-shift staffing and on-call roster; no mutual aid; ETRs through the OMS, outage line and email alerts from one minute after the start.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Limited Major Event: May 21, 2022
sources.supports: Derecho began 3:36 pm May 21, 2022; 90% of interrupted customers restored by 6:00 pm May 28; 180,946 customers interrupted on the day plus 11,528 on later days (54% of customers); about 450 workers including four high-voltage lines contractors, four neighbouring utilities, three forestry, three civil and one communications contractor; mutual assistance through Electricity Canada and EDA channels; no equipment or material shortages; outage map withdrawn and relaunched May 30 with restoration estimates in days; daily SAIDI 2,308.27 against an IEEE 1366 threshold of 5.05; only a Severe Thunderstorm Watch at 2:12 pm before outages began; company-wide debrief under way.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Limited Major Event: June 18, 2022
sources.supports: Cable fault on a Hydro One 115 kV supply; 27,405 customers (8%); 90% restored in 2 h 40 min; no warning; full on-shift complement and on-call roster; no mutual aid; first tweet 26 minutes and OMS ETRs 34 minutes after the start.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Limited Major Event: December 23, 2022
sources.supports: Winter storm with a Hydro One supply circuit trip and loss of supply to four stations; 67,710 customers interrupted (19%); 90% restored in 12 h 30 min; weather statement, watch and warning issued days ahead; on-call staff reported at 18:00 the evening before and all line and underground staff at 06:00; Incident Command Centre activated; no mutual aid; ETRs on outage map, outage line and email alerts.

sources.title: How Hydro Ottawa powers through summer storm season
sources.supports: Additional staff put on standby and resources relocated when severe weather is forecast; outages reported through the 24/7 outage line, app and MyAccount; outage map updated every 15 minutes; restoration estimates posted when available.

sources.title: How utilities prepare for emergencies
sources.supports: Emergency Response Plan with year-round simulations; priorities set by health and safety risk, essential services such as hospitals and schools, then densely populated areas; system operators in the control centre on duty 24/7; field operators handle emergency response, outage restoration and single-customer calls; on-call staff, contractors and arborists after hours; automated field devices restore some customers automatically.

sources.title: Control Room Operator (job posting, closed February 13, 2022)
sources.publisher: Oakville Hydro, via The MEARIE Group careers site
sources.supports: Ontario distribution control room duties: operate SCADA/ADMS and automated field devices, prepare and direct scheduled and emergency switching and load transfers, deliver Utility Work Protection Code processes, liaise with Hydro One and the IESO on outages and restoration, daily KPI reporting and post-event analysis; MEARIE operator training.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa releases its After the Storm report
sources.supports: May 2022 derecho: winds up to 190 km/h; damage across the entire service territory; 1,000 individual outages against 200 after the 2018 tornadoes; more than 1,500 known or reported tree contacts; 180,000 customers out at the peak; estimated cost $23.8M.

sources.title: 600 skilled field workers dispersed across city to restore remaining 29,000 customers - 3:00 PM update
sources.supports: About 600 employees and crews working around the clock; 151,000 restored six days after the storm; switching largely done remotely by the System Office; homes with damaged electrical equipment need repairs before reconnection; stay 10 metres from downed lines and call the outage line.

sources.title: Keys to the Utility Work Protection Code (IHSA Health and Safety Magazine)
sources.supports: The Electrical Utility Safety Rules govern how workers act near hazards and the Utility Work Protection Code uses permits and tags to show when lines are isolated and safe to work on; permit issuers and workers need training and certification. Publication year not stated on the page.

assumptions: A case is one IEEE 1366 Major Event Day reported to the OEB. Nine occurred in 2019-2022, so the volume is 0.19 a month, almost twice the organisation file's mode of 0.1.

Restoration labour (crews repairing poles, transformers and wires) is in edu-ops-outage-restoration through its storm surge; this workflow holds only the command, call-out, assessment, logistics, communications and reporting work, plus a line crew and bucket truck occupancy figure on the operational-period step to show the fleet tied up.

Only three of nine events activated incident command and only one (the May 2022 derecho) used mutual aid, so most simulated cases follow the control-room path. Five of nine were loss-of-supply events from Hydro One rather than storms on the distribution system.
The cycle time runs to the OEB filing, so it is dominated by report drafting and sign-off waits; restoration itself takes hours in most events and about seven days in the derecho.

Simulated time from the first warning to the start of clean-up is a median of about 14 hours (p90 about 75), including pre-event standby time; the six event reports that state it give 2.7 to 12.5 hours to restore 90% of customers in ordinary major events and about 170 hours in the derecho.
The trigger share from Hydro One (10%) covers planned or forced supply outages that become major events without a storm, as in October 2020.

FTEs are small because events are rare (about 2.3 a year); during an event most of the operations division works on it. Emergency plan upkeep and the annual drills mentioned in the event reports are not counted here.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file (wage x 1.40). Hydro Ottawa's After the Storm report PDF could not be retrieved, so figures from it are taken only from its news release.
